$comment: What the Flask (Python) reference implementation claims, and the evidence for every requirement not proven by a conformance case. Checked by apps/playground-flask/test/conformance/report.test.ts; rendered to docs/conformance-flask.md.
title: Flask (Python) reference implementation

supports.title: Flask 3 + Python 3.11+ (a Python port of the core)
PostgreSQL via psycopg 3 (the same migration SQL as the TypeScript apps; a small migration runner in Python)
MySQL 8 or MariaDB via PyMySQL (the schema derived from the PostgreSQL reference; a small migration runner in Python)
SQLite via sqlite3 (standard library): one file on one host, no server (the schema derived from the PostgreSQL reference)
MongoDB 6+ via PyMongo (the same collections and documents as the TypeScript store; indexes, not migrations)
Vue 3 (generated as client/ next to the Flask server in server/; browser-tested against the Flask server)
React (generated as client/ next to the Flask server in server/; browser-tested against the Flask server)

limitations: Every database is claimed at authorization level, not production: the production profile has not been reviewed for the Flask adapter. MySQL, SQLite and MongoDB are held to the same 90 cases as PostgreSQL, on a real server (SQLite needs none).
`selfauth add` does not work on existing Python projects (new projects only). A Vue or React frontend is generated as `client/` next to the Flask server in `server/`.
The in-memory store loses data on restart and keeps rate limits per process. It is capped at authorization level and is not for production.
The migration runner does not detect destructive statements in a way that blocks (it is reviewed by `selfauth db plan`): read every migration before applying it.

Three implementations of the core now exist. The conformance suite detects drift in the behaviour it covers; behaviour outside the cases is covered by the Python unit tests and review. Known differences (trusted proxies as false, a hop count or a list of addresses, simple case folding of email addresses, trailing slashes) are listed in apps/playground-flask/README.md.
Email and password only. No OAuth, social login, MFA or passkeys (optional capabilities, not built).
The mailer is a stub: you must implement create_mailer before production, and the server refuses to start in production without one.
Production-profile status is not claimed for Flask: the adapter has had no review except its author's. The sign-offs below are self-assessed, and no independent security audit has been done.
SQLite is one file on one host: its rate limits are not shared across application instances. Use PostgreSQL, MySQL or MongoDB to run several instances.

On MySQL a migration file that fails halfway leaves its earlier statements in place (MySQL commits DDL as it goes): restore from a backup, fix the file and run it again. MongoDB has no migrations; `migrate up` creates the missing indexes and never drops one.

signoffs.finding: docs/data-retention.md lists what deletion clears, deletes, revokes and keeps, how long, and how to purge it; checked against delete_account in the Python core (app/auth/service.py) and the migration SQL, which is the same schema as the TypeScript apps.

The store contract test makes the role link fail and asserts no user or credential remains; it runs against the in-memory and SQLite stores always, and PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB when their server is configured (CI), where creation is one transaction or one document.
A test counts Argon2 evaluations: a login for an account that does not exist costs exactly as many as a login with a wrong password.

Login calls verify_dummy on the no-user path and has no early return before password verification; the dummy hash is computed when the hasher is built, so the first unknown login costs no more than the rest.
A test counts Argon2 evaluations: registering an address that already has an account costs the same as a new one.
Register hashes the password before looking the email up, so every path costs the same.

The example route is guarded and tested anonymously; routes on auth.protected(...) deny every request that no guard allows (tested). Unlike the TypeScript apps there is no test that fails on any unguarded route in application code: that remains a review item.
Config validation rejects malformed permission names.
Config validation rejects project permissions using the reserved 'auth.' prefix.
Config validation rejects roles that reference undefined permissions.
require_permission with an undefined permission raises when the route is defined.
Role and permission sync is exercised against every reachable store and never prunes assignments: a user keeps a role that disappeared from the configuration.
Roles are synchronized by the seed command only; a database store does no sync at startup (the in-memory store is synchronized on start because it holds no data).
CT-IDENT-007 asserts the stored verifier is an Argon2id PHC string.
Hashing is argon2-cffi's low-level Argon2id (hash_secret_raw, Type.ID); there is no hand-written implementation, and verification compares in constant time (hmac.compare_digest).
A test shows the number of concurrent Argon2 runs is capped by a bounded semaphore, so a burst of requests cannot exhaust memory; the server's thread pool is bounded too.
Config validation rejects minLength below 8.
No setting or code path expires or rotates passwords; the password block of the configuration has only length, common-password and hashing keys, and a test rejects an added age key.

Tests assert the verification link carries the token in the fragment (never a query string) and that auth responses send a no-referrer policy. Rendering email-link pages is the frontend's job (the reference frontends are tested separately).
build_auth refuses an insecure session cookie and an http base URL when APP_ENV is production.

The Flask backend never redirects: no handler issues a Location header, and trailing-slash and slash-merging redirects are disabled (strict_slashes with merge_slashes off). Redirect handling after sign-in belongs to a frontend.

A test sends hostile redirect and next parameters and odd paths (double slashes, trailing slashes, encoded dots) and asserts no response is a redirect or carries a Location header. It found Werkzeug's default slash merging redirecting '/api//x', which is now off.
The security workflow runs gitleaks over the full history on every push and pull request and weekly; the configuration has no secret fields.
The configuration is decoded strictly and has no field that holds a secret (a test checks the defaults and that an added secret key is rejected); secrets come from environment variables.
A test asserts the generated .env.example holds placeholders only and .gitignore covers .env.
Tests assert start-up fails without a valid SELFAUTH_APP_BASE_URL, and that token-mode CSRF cannot start without a secret of at least 32 bytes.
Tests assert CSRF secrets under 32 bytes are refused, tokens signed with the previous secret are still accepted, and tokens signed with a dropped secret are refused.
The previous secret is verified but never used to sign, so rotation cannot keep an old key alive.
The Store contract can only append security events (record_event), and no route or service updates or deletes one.
The options that reveal registered emails are off in the default configuration, and sign-in after registration is rejected unless the reveal option is on.
The customization guide describes the revealExistingEmail trade-off.
selfauth doctor warns when revealExistingEmail is enabled in a Flask project's selfauth.config.json.
The deployment guide requires HTTPS and shows the HSTS header; build_auth and the environment loader refuse an http base URL in production.
A test asserts the unique indexes exist on a fresh database, and the store contract test shows concurrent registrations of one address create one account.
Migrations are applied and verified on a fresh database by the project's migration runner: once, idempotently, with edited migrations refused and a failing file changing nothing on SQLite.
The application never migrates or seeds at startup; migrations are applied only by the explicit migrate command.
A test migrates a database that already holds an application table with rows and asserts they are untouched and that every other table is SelfAuth's own (auth_ prefix).
Every error carries a stable code; no Python code matches message text (errors are AuthError with a code), and the conformance runner branches on error.code.
The configuration is decoded with unknown fields rejected; tests reject unknown top-level and nested keys.
Unknown keys are rejected, so a secret cannot be added to the config file.
No field in the configuration carries a secret.
Out-of-range TTLs, lengths and timeouts are rejected, not clamped.
The store factory rejects a configuration naming a database this project does not have built in.
Config validation rejects an unsupported major specVersion.
